etymology: From Latin probitas, from probo, to prove. Webster 1828 names tried virtue or integrity: strict honesty, sincerity, and veracity in principle.
biblical_def: Probity is tried integrity: strict honesty that conforms actions to the laws of justice. The integrity of the upright shall guide them (Pro 11:3). The just man walketh in his integrity (Pro 20:7). It is not a public pose. It is proved in dealings the courts never see.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PROB'ITY as tried virtue or integrity; in general, strict honesty, sincerity, veracity, and integrity in principle.
webster_full: PROB'ITY, noun [Latin probitas, from probo, to prove.] Primarily, tried virtue or integrity, or approved actions; but in general, strict honesty; sincerity; veracity; integrity in principle, or strict conformity of actions to the laws of justice. Probity of mind or principle is best evinced by probity of conduct in social dealings, particularly in adhering to strict integrity in the observance and performance of rights called imperfect, which public laws do not reach and cannot enforce.
scriptures: Proverbs 11:3
The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them.
Proverbs 20:7
The just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him.
corruption_summary: Probity is now often reduced to compliance, optics, or a brand of honesty, as if the unenforced right were no duty.
corruption_paragraphs: A man can clear an audit and still defraud the right no statute reaches. Webster named that case. Probity is strict conformity to justice where public laws cannot enforce it.
The other dodge calls integrity a private feeling. Scripture calls it a walk. The just man walketh in his integrity, and his children are blessed after him.
roots_summary: Latin probitas is proved honesty. The KJV speaks of integrity that guides and of a just man who walks in it. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin probo — to prove; tried virtue.
KJV integrity guides the upright (Pro 11:3).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun probity.
usage: Probity is tried honesty, not a public pose.
The unenforced right is still a duty.
The just man walketh in his integrity.

etymology: From Latin supercilium, the eyebrow, hence a raised brow of disdain. Webster 1828 names haughtiness, and an overbearing temper or manner.
biblical_def: Superciliousness is haughtiness: an overbearing temper that looks down. Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall (Pro 16:18). The haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted (Isa 2:11). A raised brow is not wisdom. It is pride waiting for a fall.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SUPERCIL'IOUSNESS as haughtiness; an overbearing temper or manner.
webster_full: SUPERCIL'IOUSNESS, noun Haughtiness; an overbearing temper or manner.
scriptures: Proverbs 16:18
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Isaiah 2:11
The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.
corruption_summary: Superciliousness is now often rebranded as standards, taste, or confidence, as if an overbearing manner were a virtue.
corruption_paragraphs: A man can call his raised brow discernment. Webster named it haughtiness. An overbearing temper is not a gift of judgment. It is pride.
Isaiah does not leave the lofty look standing. The haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.
roots_summary: Latin supercilium is the eyebrow lifted in disdain. The KJV names a haughty spirit and the haughtiness of men. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin supercilium — eyebrow; a look of disdain.
KJV haughty spirit goeth before a fall (Pro 16:18).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun superciliousness.
usage: Superciliousness is an overbearing temper, not high standards.
A haughty spirit goeth before a fall.
The LORD alone shall be exalted.

etymology: From knave, a dishonest fellow. Webster 1828 names dishonesty, deception in traffick, trick, petty villainy, and fraud.
biblical_def: Knavery is dishonesty in dealing: trick, fraud, and petty villainy. A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight (Pro 11:1). The wicked man's mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud (Psa 10:7). Clever trade does not baptize a trick. God hates the false weight.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines KNA'VERY as dishonesty; deception in traffick; trick; petty villainy; fraud; also mischievous tricks or practices.
webster_full: KNA'VERY, noun na'very. Dishonesty; deception in traffick; trick; petty villainy; fraud.
scriptures: Proverbs 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
Psalm 10:7
His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud: under his tongue is mischief and vanity.
corruption_summary: Knavery is now often praised as hustle or sharp dealing, as if deception in traffick were skill rather than fraud.
corruption_paragraphs: A false balance can be called margin, growth, or the way business works. Webster named it deception in traffick. The LORD calls it abomination.
The other dodge shrinks knavery to a prank. Mischievous tricks that cheat a neighbor are still fraud. Under the tongue of the wicked is mischief and vanity.
roots_summary: English knave names the dishonest man. The KJV condemns a false balance and a mouth full of fraud. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: English knave — a dishonest fellow; trick in trade.
KJV false balance is abomination (Pro 11:1).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun knavery.
usage: Knavery is deception in traffick, not clever trade.
A false balance is abomination to the LORD.
A trick that cheats a neighbor is fraud.

etymology: From villain, a base fellow. Webster 1828 names extreme depravity and atrocious wickedness, and also a crime of deep depravity.
biblical_def: Villainy is extreme depravity: atrocious wickedness, not a costume. GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually (Gen 6:5). The soul of the wicked desireth evil (Pro 21:10). The word names the deed and the heart that wills it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines VIL'LAINY as extreme depravity and atrocious wickedness, and also as a crime, an action of deep depravity.
webster_full: VIL'LAINY, noun 1. Extreme depravity; atrocious wickedness; as the villany of the thief or the robber; the villany of the seducer.
2. A crime; an action of deep depravity. In this sense, the word has a plural.
scriptures: Genesis 6:5
And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
Proverbs 21:10
The soul of the wicked desireth evil: his neighbour findeth no favour in his eyes.
corruption_summary: Villainy is now often worn as style, antihero, or brand, as if deep depravity were a costume rather than a crime.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture can cheer the robber and the seducer if the lighting is right. Webster named their work villany: extreme depravity, atrocious wickedness. Genesis does not call that imagination art. It was only evil continually.
The other dodge reserves the word for monsters and excuses the neighbor-crushing heart. The soul of the wicked desireth evil. Deep depravity is a crime, whether or not a crowd applauds it.
roots_summary: English villain names the base man. The KJV speaks of wickedness great in the earth, and of a soul that desireth evil. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: English villain — a base fellow; atrocious wickedness.
KJV wickedness of man was great (Gen 6:5).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun villainy.
usage: Villainy is extreme depravity, not a costume.
The imagination only evil continually is not art.
A crime of deep depravity keeps its name.

etymology: From Latin candor, brightness, whiteness, hence openness. Webster 1828 names openness of heart, frankness, and freedom from tricks or disguise.
biblical_def: Candor is openness of heart: frankness without tricks or disguise. In simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, the apostles had their conversation (2Co 1:12). Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight (Pro 12:22). Openness is not cruelty. It is freedom from disguise.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CANDOR as openness of heart; frankness; ingenuousness; a disposition to treat subjects with fairness; freedom from tricks or disguise; sincerity.
webster_full: CANDOR, noun Openness of heart; frankness; ingenuousness of mind; a disposition to treat subjects with fairness; freedom from tricks or disguise; sincerity.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 1:12

For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward.
Proverbs 12:22
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
corruption_summary: Candor is now often used as a license for cruelty, or staged as transparency, as if openness of heart were either a weapon or a performance.
corruption_paragraphs: A man can call spite candor and demand thanks for the wound. Webster named fairness and freedom from tricks, not a right to be savage. Godly sincerity is not fleshly wisdom with the gloves off.
The other dodge performs openness and keeps the disguise. Lying lips are still abomination. They that deal truly are the LORD's delight.
roots_summary: Latin candor is brightness, hence an open mind. The KJV commends godly sincerity and dealing truly. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin candor — brightness; openness of heart.
KJV godly sincerity, not fleshly wisdom (2Co 1:12).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun candor.
usage: Candor is openness without disguise, not a license to wound.
Godly sincerity is not fleshly wisdom.
They that deal truly are the LORD's delight.

etymology: From Latin animositas, from animus, spirit or passion. Webster 1828 names violent hatred with active opposition: active enmity.
biblical_def: Animosity is violent hatred joined to active opposition. The works of the flesh include hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, and strife (Gal 5:20). We were sometimes hateful, and hating one another (Tit 3:3). It is not a private opinion. It is enmity that moves to oppose, and it belongs to the old life.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ANIMOS'ITY as violent hatred accompanied with active opposition; active enmity, distinct from secret enmity and from malice.
webster_full: ANIMOS'ITY, noun [Latin animositas; animosus, animated, courageous, enraged; from animus, spirit, mind, passion.] Violent hatred accompanied with active opposition; active enmity. Animosity differs from enmity which may be secret and inactive; and it expresses a less criminal passion than malice. Animosity seeks to gain a cause or destroy an enemy or rival, from hatred or private interest; malice seeks revenge for the sake of giving pain.
scriptures: Galatians 5:20
Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies,
Titus 3:3
For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
corruption_summary: Animosity is now often baptized as passion, voice, or a cause, as if active hatred were a duty once the rival is named.
corruption_paragraphs: A cause can be just and the hatred still be of the flesh. Webster named violent hatred with active opposition. Galatians lists hatred, variance, wrath, and strife among the works of the flesh, beside idolatry.
The other dodge calls animosity honesty about enemies. Titus names the old life: hateful, and hating one another. Active enmity is not sanctified by a slogan.
roots_summary: Latin animus is spirit or passion. The KJV lists hatred and strife as works of the flesh, and hating one another as the old life. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin animositas — violent hatred with active opposition.
KJV hatred, variance, wrath, strife are works of the flesh (Gal 5:20).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun animosity.
usage: Animosity is active enmity, not a righteous cause.
Hatred and strife are works of the flesh.
The old life hates. It is not a virtue.

etymology: From Latin beneficentia, from benefacio, to do good. Webster 1828 names the practice of doing good: active goodness, kindness, or charity.
biblical_def: Beneficence is the practice of doing good, not a wish to be thought kind. As we have opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith (Gal 6:10). The Lord went about doing good (Act 10:38). Charity that never acts is not the thing Webster named, and not the thing Paul commanded.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BENEF'ICENCE as the practice of doing good; active goodness, kindness, or charity.
webster_full: BENEF'ICENCE, noun [Latin beneficentia, from the participle of benefacio.] The practice of doing good; active goodness, kindness, or charity.
scriptures: Galatians 6:10
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
Acts 10:38
How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.
corruption_summary: Beneficence is now often staged as brand kindness, as if being seen to care were the same as the practice of doing good.
corruption_paragraphs: A gift can be announced and never reach the weak. Webster named active goodness. Paul names opportunity: do good unto all men, especially the household of faith. The practice is the word.
The other dodge waits for a perfect cause and calls delay wisdom. The Lord went about doing good. Active charity does not need a crowd.
roots_summary: Latin benefacio is to do good. The KJV commands doing good as there is opportunity, and records the Lord going about doing good. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin benefacio — to do good; active charity.
KJV do good unto all men (Gal 6:10).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun beneficence.
usage: Beneficence is the practice of doing good, not the wish.
Do good unto all men, especially the household of faith.
Active charity does not need a crowd.

etymology: From Latin diffidentia, from diffido, to distrust. Webster 1828 names distrust of others, and more generally distrust of one's self.
biblical_def: Diffidence is distrust. Distrust of one's own sufficiency is wisdom: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding (Pro 3:5). We are not sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God (2Co 3:5). Distrust of God is another thing, and it is sin. The word must not be used to baptize unbelief.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DIFFIDENCE as distrust and want of confidence; more generally, distrust of one's self, issuing in reserve, modesty, or bashfulness.
webster_full: DIFFIDENCE, noun [Latin diffidentia, from diffido, to distrust.] 1. Distrust; want of confidence; any doubt of the power, ability or disposition of others.
2. More generally, distrust of one's self; want of confidence in our own power, competency, correctness or wisdom; a doubt respecting some personal qualification.
3. Modest reserve; a moderate degree of timidity or bashfulness.
scriptures: Proverbs 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
2 Corinthians 3:5
Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God;
corruption_summary: Diffidence is now often treated as a defect to be cured, as if distrust of self were sickness and trust in one's own heart were health.
corruption_paragraphs: The age tells a man to trust himself and calls distrust of self a flaw. Scripture reverses the counsel. Lean not unto thine own understanding. Our sufficiency is of God.
The other error uses diffidence to cover unbelief, as if doubting the LORD were humility. It is not. Diffidence toward one's own heart is faith's posture. Diffidence toward God is departure from him.
roots_summary: Latin diffido is to distrust. The KJV commands trust in the LORD and denies that we are sufficient of ourselves. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin diffido — to distrust; want of confidence in self.
KJV lean not unto thine own understanding (Pro 3:5).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun diffidence.
usage: Diffidence toward self is wisdom. Diffidence toward God is sin.
Lean not unto thine own understanding.
Our sufficiency is of God.
